content: Periodontal disease has been associated with various systemic conditions, including cardiovascular disease, stroke, diabetes, and adverse pregnancy outcomes. These associations are thought to occur through systemic inflammatory pathways. Periodontal disease is particularly common among women of reproductive age, and gum conditions often worsen during pregnancy. Observational studies have suggested that treating periodontal disease may reduce the risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. However, a comprehensive review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) is necessary to evaluate the effects of periodontal treatment on maternal and perinatal health outcomes. The objective of this review was to assess whether treating periodontal disease in pregnant women can prevent or reduce maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Trials Register, Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS, up to October 6, 2016. Ongoing trials were also identified through ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. The review included RCTs that investigated the effects of periodontal treatment on maternal and perinatal outcomes. Studies that did not report obstetric outcomes were excluded. Data were independently extracted by two reviewers, and missing information was obtained by contacting study authors. The risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane's 'Risk of bias' tool, and the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Where appropriate, results from comparable trials were pooled using a random-effects model and expressed as risk ratios (RR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Fifteen RCTs involving 7,161 participants met the inclusion criteria. Most studies were at high risk of bias due to issues such as lack of blinding and imbalances in baseline characteristics. The participants were pregnant women with periodontitis (14 studies) or gingivitis (1 study) recruited from prenatal care facilities. The studies primarily compared periodontal treatment with no treatment during pregnancy or compared different types of periodontal treatments. Eleven studies compared periodontal treatment with no treatment during pregnancy. The meta-analysis showed no clear difference in the risk of preterm birth before 37 weeks (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.10; 5,671 participants; low-quality evidence). There was low-quality evidence suggesting that periodontal treatment may reduce the risk of low birth weight (< 2500 g) (9.7% with treatment vs. 12.6% without treatment; RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.95; 3,470 participants; 7 studies). However, it remains unclear whether periodontal treatment affects the risk of preterm birth before 35 weeks (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.76; 2,557 participants; 2 studies) or before 32 weeks (RR 1.35, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.32; 2,755 participants; 3 studies). Similarly, there was no clear evidence of an effect on very low birth weight (< 1500 g) (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.70; 2,550 participants; 2 studies), perinatal mortality (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.43; 5,320 participants; 7 studies; very low-quality evidence), or pre-eclampsia (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.62; 2,946 participants; 3 studies; very low-quality evidence). There was also no evidence of a difference in the risk of small-for-gestational-age infants (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.16; 3,610 participants; 3 studies; low-quality evidence). Four studies compared different types of periodontal treatments, such as more intensive versus less intensive interventions. Due to clinical heterogeneity, data pooling was not possible. The reported outcomes included preterm birth before 37 weeks, preterm birth before 35 weeks, low birth weight (< 2500 g), very low birth weight (< 1500 g), and perinatal mortality. However, the quality of evidence for these comparisons was very low, and it remains unclear whether one type of periodontal treatment is superior to another. None of the studies reported maternal mortality or adverse effects of the interventions. In conclusion, it is uncertain whether periodontal treatment during pregnancy reduces the risk of preterm birth (low-quality evidence). There is low-quality evidence suggesting that periodontal treatment may reduce the risk of low birth weight (< 2500 g), but the confidence in this estimate is limited. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether one type of periodontal treatment is more effective than another in preventing adverse obstetric outcomes. Future research should aim to report both periodontal and obstetric outcomes to provide more robust evidence.
